paragraphs.heading: A wave that shakes sideways
paragraphs.text: An S wave, also called a secondary or shear wave, is one of the two main kinds of elastic body wave. Body waves get their name because they travel through the inside of an object rather than along its surface. S waves are transverse: the particles they disturb move at right angles to the direction the wave is going. The force that pulls the material back into place comes mainly from shear stress.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is called secondary
paragraphs.text: In solids, S waves move more slowly than the compressional primary waves, or P waves. So on an earthquake seismograph they are the second type of wave to show up, after the P wave. That order of arrival is where the name secondary comes from.

paragraphs.heading: What it cannot cross
paragraphs.text: Because they depend on shear, S waves cannot travel through gases. They also cannot move through liquids that have zero or very low viscosity, although thick, highly viscous liquids can carry them. Inside the Earth, this means S waves are blocked by the molten outer core. That leaves a shadow zone for S waves on the side of the planet opposite where they started.

paragraphs.heading: Clues from the inner core
paragraphs.text: S waves can still exist in the solid inner core. When a P wave hits the boundary between the molten and solid cores at a slant, it gives rise to S waves that travel through the solid. When those S waves reach the boundary again at a slant, they create P waves that carry on through the liquid. Seismologists use this behaviour to work out some physical properties of the inner core.

paragraphs.heading: An idea from 1830
paragraphs.text: In 1830 the mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson presented a theory of elastic waves in solids to the French Academy of Sciences. He said an earthquake would send out two different waves, one with a speed a and the other with a speed a/√3. Far from the source, the first kind squeezes and stretches the material along its direction of travel. The second kind stretches the material across that direction.

paragraphs.heading: Shear waves in medicine
paragraphs.text: Shear waves also have a use in medicine. Magnetic resonance elastography, or MRE, studies living tissue by sending shear waves through it with a vibrator and watching the response with magnetic resonance imaging. Measuring how fast the waves move and how long they are reveals elastic properties such as the shear modulus. MRE has been used to study liver, brain and bone.
